rate.text: Big US surveys and long studies agree that many people recover, but most figures come second-hand, through reviews that didn't check the studies' quality. For drugs other than alcohol, none of the sources we read counted who recovered without treatment.
rate.reason: Three sentences where one or two are asked; 'nobody here' is unclear to a reader and reads as a statement about all research; the main reason for the downgrade (second-hand estimates from reviews that did not appraise their studies) was only half given.

rate.text: One big survey, chosen to stand for all US adults living at home. But it's people's own answers, which nobody checked, and 'misuse' counts taking extra of your own pills the same as taking pills to get high.
rate.reason: Who was not asked (institutions, the military) is the claim's scope, not a reason the domains or reasoning give for the rating, and 'such as prisons' is not in the claim; the broad definition of misuse, which the risk-of-bias note does give, replaces it, and the scope moves into the first sentence.

rate.text: Two big reviews, but few trials tested the two drugs against each other, and none in adults. Trials lasted weeks, only about 1 in 4 was clearly well run, and in one review most were paid for by drug makers.
rate.reason: Industry funding (87 of 102 trials) is given only for the blood-pressure review, not for both; the main risk-of-bias reason (only about a quarter of trials at low risk, most unclear) was missing.

rate.text: One set of US side-effect reports, which catch only some cases, sorted by a committee the drug's maker paid for. There was no group stopping other opioids to compare with.
rate.reason: 'Nobody compared' speaks for all research; the claim says only that this series had no group stopping another opioid.

item.statement: Blotters taken as LSD always hold LSD.
item.why: In some reported cases, blotters taken as 'acid' held an NBOMe instead. These reports don't show how often this happens.

quiz.reason: 'Nobody has counted how often' speaks for all research; the claim says only that its sources did not measure it. Same fix as the 'but' line.

item.statement: Published NBOMe cases had far more seizures than cases reported to poison centres.
item.why: About 38 in 100 published cases had seizures, against 1 of 25 cases reported to Texas poison centres. Published cases are often the worst ones.

quiz.reason: '4 in 100 of 25 cases' is confusing; 1 of 25 is the same figure said plainly (lines: 4 in 100 of 25 cases). 'Poison centre cases' made plainer.

Its subject is how much Suboxone it takes to block other opioids: an amount, in a mixing context, not framed as a risk fact. Its why ('early modelling of a few volunteers') is not in the lines. Without the amount it becomes a technical point about receptor thresholds, not worth a reader's time.

item.statement: In a lab test, people rated trips on LSD and on psilocybin, the drug in magic mushrooms, alike on most measures.
item.why: In 28 people, most ratings barely differed, though LSD lasted longer. But that's no proof they're the same, and most could tell which drug they'd had.

quiz.reason: 'As much alike' left out the one big difference the lines lead with (how long it lasts, itself measured from people's ratings); 'alike on most measures' is the short line's own hedge.

how: In three US surveys from 1990 to 2003, 76 to 83 in 100 people who had ever been dependent on a drug no longer counted as dependent in the past year. They could still use drugs, or relapse later.

Counted one drug at a time, half of people dependent on cocaine had recovered within about 4 years of becoming dependent, cannabis 6, alcohol 16 and cigarettes 30. Some stayed dependent for decades. Heroin wasn't in these figures.
Of US soldiers addicted to narcotics in Vietnam, 5 in 100 were addicted again in their first year home and 12 in 100 within 3 years. Few entered drug treatment back home.

In 21 long studies, mostly of people found through treatment, 54 in 100 of those followed to the end were in recovery (35 in 100 of everyone who started). For alcohol, counts of recovery without treatment run from 3 to 98 in 100, mostly because studies count different groups.

lines.reason: '35 to 54 in 100' read as a range across studies, but the two figures are two denominators: 54% of people followed to the end, 35% of everyone enrolled with deaths and losses counted as not recovered (the statement's point that the number depends on who is counted).

fields.but: These reports don't show how often 'LSD' blotters hold NBOMes. And they're reports of people who got sick, so they can't say how risky one use is.
how: NBOMes are lab-made relatives of the 2C drugs. Of the first 10 found in Europe, from 2011 to 2013, 8 were on blotters. In some cases, blotters taken as 'acid' turned out to hold an NBOMe.
In 29 published cases of poisoning, nearly all had a racing heart and about 4 in 10 had seizures. Some needed intensive care, a breathing machine or dialysis.
Published cases are often the worst ones. Of 25 cases reported to Texas poison centres, 1 had seizures, against about 4 in 10 published cases.
By 2014, eight deaths had been reported with 25I-NBOMe, and a lab found it in five. Some had taken other drugs too. The review says its role in the deaths was often unclear.

lines.reason: 'Nobody has counted' speaks for all research; the statement says only that it was not measured in the review's sources (reasoning: 'nothing here measures'). '4 in 100' of 25 cases is 1 case: said as a count so the small number shows.

how: In a US survey in 2015 and 2016, about 13 in 100 adults had used a benzo in the past year. About 2 in 100 had misused one. At ages 18 to 25, about half of all benzo use was misuse.
Misuse meant any use a doctor didn't direct. Most often (74 in 100) it was pills without a prescription. Three in four had misused alprazolam (Xanax).
Main reasons: relaxing 47 in 100, sleep 27, getting high 12, coping with feelings 10. All the reasons together add up to a bit over 100; the paper doesn't say if people could pick more than one.
About 69 in 100 got the pills from a friend or relative, mostly for free, and 20 in 100 from one doctor. About 7 in 100 met the criteria for dependence.

lines.reason: 'These add up to a bit over 100' was wrong for the four listed (they add to 96); it is all seven reasons that add to 103.6. The statement says the paper does not say whether people could give more than one main reason, not that it doesn't say why.

fields.short: Both work. In a review of 133 short trials, amphetamine (as in Adderall) eased symptoms a bit more than methylphenidate (Ritalin). Quitting over side effects didn't clearly differ between them.
how: A review pooled 133 trials in about 14,300 children and teens and 10,300 adults. On doctors' ratings at up to about 12 weeks, amphetamine eased symptoms a little more than methylphenidate. The review rated this low certainty.

Quitting because of side effects wasn't clearly different between the two, but a gap wasn't ruled out. Against a dummy pill, more quit on amphetamine at every age, and on methylphenidate in adults. Both lowered weight.

Over about 7 weeks, blood pressure rose by about 1 to 3 points and heart rate by about 2 to 5 beats a minute on average, compared with a dummy pill. The two drugs didn't clearly differ, in 102 trials.

One blinded trial gave 125 children each drug for two weeks, at one set dose, with no dummy pill. Parents counted about as many complaints on each, but rated sleep and mood ones a bit worse on dexamphetamine (an amphetamine). Many, like irritability (82 in 100), were there before any medicine.

lines.reason: Short: 'Neither clearly made more people quit' did not name the comparison and can be read as against a dummy pill, where more people did quit (amphetamine at all ages, methylphenidate in adults). How 1: the analyses took the time closest to 12 weeks, in trials often shorter, so not 'after about 12 weeks'. How 4: the counts were about the same (7.6 against 7.2), not the same, and the statement says the severity gap may reflect the one fixed dose of each.

how: 28 healthy adults each had five hospital days, at least 10 days apart. They got a dummy, two amounts of LSD and two of psilocybin, in random order, not told which.
LSD lasted longer at both amounts. The authors think that's because it stays in the blood longer, but they didn't test this.

The higher psilocybin amount raised blood pressure and body temperature a little more; the higher LSD amount raised heart rate more. On a checklist, 13 to 18 of the 28 had a headache in the first 12 hours after the drugs, against 8 on the dummy. Nobody had a serious problem.
People named the right drug after 71 to 86 in 100 sessions, and the dummy after every session, which may have shaped their ratings. It used pure psilocybin in capsules, not mushrooms.

lines.reason: The onset point compared forms for speed (a liquid starting sooner than a capsule), close to the forms-and-routes comparison the site shows only in an approved section 7; the statement's own explanation of the main finding (LSD's longer half-life, given without a formal test) is more useful in its place.

fields.but: Each study had 3 to 10 volunteers dependent on heroin, not in treatment. Fentanyl and overdose weren't studied.
how: In brain scans of people dependent on heroin, the higher the daily dose of buprenorphine (Suboxone's main drug), the fewer opioid receptors were left free. At 16 mg a day, 9 to 20 in 100 were still free 4 hours after a dose.
Even at the highest doses tested, heroin and another opioid still had some effect. The review mentions people who take more of them to get past the block, but has no data on what happens then.
After 10 volunteers stopped 16 mg a day, free receptors rose from about 13 to 25 in 100 at 4 hours to about 75 to 90 in 100 at 3 days. These figures come from curves drawn between 4 scans.
The review's summary gives receptor levels needed to block other opioids. But its own authors say nobody knows them. A full block was never reliably seen.

lines.reason: How 1 said buprenorphine 'took up more opioid receptors', but the statement says the scans measure receptors left free (availability), not receptors taken up, which equal each other only under assumptions. But: 'volunteers on heroin' can read as under its influence; the studies were of people dependent on heroin. For the editors: the question's 'for how long' is answered with a time course after the last dose (how 3); it is in the claim, but check that it cannot read as timing for using other opioids.

fields.but: It's only cases people chose to report. And there was no group stopping other opioids to compare with.
how: Of 1,248 side-effect reports in tramadol's first five years in the US, 422 were counted as withdrawal after stopping. Most were the usual kind: cramps, diarrhoea, goose bumps, a runny nose, sweating, poor sleep.

55 (about 1 in 8) had more: bad anxiety or panic (1 in 3 of them), confusion or feeling unreal (1 in 4), numbness or tingling (1 in 4), or hallucinations (1 in 5). The researchers say this could be mistaken for psychosis.
Most people whose dose was known had taken no more than the recommended daily maximum, and many had used tramadol only a few days. Doctors called most cases mild, usually over in 2 or 3 days.

How often withdrawal happens is unknown: the researchers cite an estimate that only about 1 in 10 side effects get reported. The drug's maker paid for the study. A review of Iranian studies found just two case reports of it.

lines.reason: 'No one compared' speaks for all research; the statement says only that these reports had no group stopping another opioid. How 1: 422 is the committee's withdrawal rating; at least 546 reports described withdrawal (124 were counted as abuse because of drug-seeking), so 'were counted as' rather than 'were'.
